segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This conversation with Helmer Ring Sage took place at his home in Moscow on February 27th, 1976. The interviewer is Sam Schrager.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And the crop footage spoiled over there. And I would have been sunk worse over there than I would have been, than I did get over here. Here I only owed a thousand to the dairy bank and I had forty-four head of cattle to ox that. They got their money's worth of, could have, if they could have sold them. Thirty-two, nineteen thirty-two men a week went down to two bits over there to park. And the only man that saved me was old President Roosevelt. Delano Roosevelt. He made the stipulation that any family man that had, regardless, if he was a fireman and had fifty, he was exempt fifty-five acres of crop for his family. No mortgage could take it. So that's what I done. I had a little oats, I don't know, thirty-two dollars worth probably is all I had. I sold pocketed of money every time I come in.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Now, Old Harsh was a nice banker. He's the one that I didn't want to borrow that much money to start with. I only wanted five hundred to buy me. I was going to, here was the deal, I didn't tell you. I'd bought a state land on terms. Eighty acres right along there in park, there close to this Nolan place. That's, well, it'd be west of where Jellibear is, up in the mountain there. Just about as soon as you enter into park, get over the top of the grate. Well anyway, I got that fourteen hundred dollars from my brother Simon, one died with cancer. He lent me the cash to make the down payment. And then I got, when I got the fireman on the ridge, you see, the first two years I was making pretty good, some of it. One year, I mean, I made good. I raised some beans on forty-four acres of ground Dad had.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And I got thirteen hundred pounds to the acre. And I come putting in missing it like some of them. One of the neighbors there, he tried to hold me, he said, oh you don't sell yet. Said the retail in Spokane, they tell me I haven't sent. Well I could have gotten nine cents. I was back a little bit. I could have gotten nine cents. But old Guernsey, I had the hall clear on the other side then. Old Guernsey, he says, you want to sell this morning ring to Hayden? I said, well I don't know. I said, what's the price? He says, nine cents. He's laughing, kind of, you know. Him and McGill was in part, you see. I thought, God damn that smile, I thought maybe he had something up his sleeve I could get a little more. I said, how about a dime? No, he said, or a dime, he said, pretty good. Well it was. I was a damn fool not taking it, see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well I held that dog dog crop. I said, pretty soon this rice here man, come down here, he want this money. He wanted it right now. I said, okay, I'll call up McGill and I wasn't going to fight him. He come and tried when I asked him to. He wanted his money, by God he had the right to get it. He said he had to pay his crew, which was nothing more than right.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long after the crop was in, was this?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, that was after I started hauling, I had it hauled down to the warehouse.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Wasn't very long after he thrashed it?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, it may be, no not too long, I don't know, maybe it was a month or two, I can't remember that for sure. But anyway, he, I called up McGill. I said, how much is beans? He kind of was a squeaky voice guy. He said, beans are coming down, there's still seven and a half cents in the dirt, you better sell. I said, well, I'll sell my share, but my dad had told me not to sell his share. Till I let him know. Now he was a dang fool for not letting McGill know when the price, and he could have told McGill here, when that price is suitable, sell. Well, he should have done it. He didn't do it. By the time I wrote to Dad and he finally fiddled around like some of the rest of the farmers to spring, he did get, he left it to McGill then and he got five cents, the rest of the farmers, beans laid in the warehouse.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: They couldn't sell them. I was dang lucky, I got that seven and a half.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Your father sold for five?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: He sold for five, his third share.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But the other farmers couldn't sell at all?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And I sold mine in the fall, you see, for the seven and a half.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The other farmers didn't sell at all?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, a lot of them didn't sell. They was vacillating. This one guy, Dan Gold, that brother's the one that trashed for us. By God, he was the one that told me about prices so good in Spokane. Fuck God, they were retailing in hell, you wouldn't go about that. Little damn farmers, these grain buyers, boy, you better listen to them. I got my lesson there. And then I went as far as one year then, by gosh, if I didn't even borrow a dollar and a half on my week. Week was a dollar and a half, I should have sold. No, I had the damn thing till the next year. You know what I got? I got the shit, the warehouse took it for storage, 84 cents. That's what put me under here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It cost 84 cents for storage?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, yeah, it amounted to that. It amounted to that. Well, that isn't counting what I borrowed. I borrowed a dollar and a half, I had to pay up… don't you see… that dollar and a half I borrowed. Dollar and a half a bushel? Yeah, I borrowed, you see, that would be 85, that would be, what? That would be 50, 65 cents extra that I overdrew, you see, that I owed the bank.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What year was that, do you know? Oh, God, there's about 19, wait now, I can put in your figure, that'll be, what year would that be?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: This was 1919 when I had the good beans. And, let's see now, 1919. No, wait, I had the beans. You see, the way I keep track is, my oldest daughter, she was born in 1918, and she was a year old. Dad was working with the bean horse, my other boys. And that year old she would, that'd be 1919, I had the good crop of beans that I sold. And I got $2,100 for my share at seven and a half cents. Now he could have got a thousand dollars for yours. No, he didn't, because he only got five cents, you see, so he lacked, oh, a couple, three hundred dollars of getting what he should have gotten.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, in a way, I got this done, and this here, this whole idea, this idea of speculation, do you think if you look back at it, did you do better to sell right away?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I did, but God, listen, then after that I did. Then what did God tell you then? I think it was 19, no, just 1919 I sold, I mean I had the big bean crop and then you're putting that on here. ... I only had 16 bushels of that market spring, you see, but it was clean. The old crop at the warehouse on this side was the man that gave me the big offer. I was coming down there, you know, he said, How much of this wheat you got, Green Sage? I said, I've got 1019 sacks, counting the old man's share… he gets a third of the wheat, see. Well, he said,… i understand, well, wheat had been going 2, 12, 12, 14, 16 long there. You told me this.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I think you told me about this. Because you got good money.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: So then, when it went, he said, now, he said, it's been jiggling up and down. He says, how will 220 strike you? Fine, I said, make it more if you want to. And, no. Let's see, wait a minute, I've got that mixed up… 220, what's that… yes, boy, gosh, a good boy. 220. And the next day I come down, he says, I understand the other warehouses give him a little more. He says, oh, yeah, that's when he said, how 2 and a quarter strike you? I said, make it 2, then. And so, that year, I got good money out of the wheat. 5,100 dollars. But dad had to have 1,700 of that, you see. But that still didn't put me out of that. Then I got fed up with wheat. I happened to have one sow in a half-maker lot. It used to be the old orchard. I planted it for pasture, but we didn't have a little sow for them. And I had a little barley.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I ground the barley, the roll that fed to this sow, and just crowded them. I wanted to see what I could do. And by golly, in five months I had 200-pound pigs. And I got to figuring on that. I said, Jesus, that peach wheat's all two pieces. That was... I beat the price for raising wheat on that little lot of ground, see. And it counted the grain that I'd had in oil. I said, man, I can just go into hogs if I can get a building. Well, first year I didn't. First year I used dad's... He had a big machine shed. And I made mistakes. Two mistakes. One was, I had to... You know, where the sows were pinned off together, partitioned off. Each sow had one sow that would eat this other sow's pigs if he hatched. She cleaned up one sow's pig or a damn near before I caught on. Well, another mistake I made that year was... We used to earn cattle the first year I was there. We had cattle. We sold them the whole... Quick, we couldn't like that. We couldn't get no person. So I said...

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I did..… now, it's salt. I put in this big cattle trough, see. Rock salt. And melted. And the pigs would come and drink that. And they died off like flies. You went down to the water... Down to the pond, right. They filled up and busted it. I didn't know what was going on. Nice, fat pigs. Just from that salt… what the hell… one of the neighbors come along there and he says... Helmer, he says, I'll tell you what's the matter… i says, what… said, we had a sow. We fed some ice cream salt. Brian. Said, an hour or two after she drank that, she bloated and died. He says, here's your trouble. He says, you got this salt trough here. He said, if you get a block salt, he said it won't happen. Boy, that's when I got busy. I only had 17 pigs left out of 85 little pigs that first year. I mean, that's the second year after I'd raised it once out. Then I got busy. Boy, that's no good. I wrote to my dad if he'd let me move a house he had on the back field, that scouting place where I had the big bean crop.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I said, could I move that over? He wanted to know how I could do it. I said, I can do it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did you do that?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: He started to tell you. I done it. I done it. I got a stump puller down. This poor little friend of mine that died last spring, Chuck Graham. His dad had a big Hercules stump puller about this high. They were all good. Them days, you know. His dad run a little sawmill up in the canyon there by Peck. Besides, he had a gristmill in Peck where I could get my flour ground. He was a nice old man. I said, I'll finish that later. He says, go ahead and use it. I took it up there and barred another neighbor west. 200 foot cable. That's 400 feet, cable. Spiced them together.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You had 200 on the stump puller?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, 200 foot cable. I had to dig three quarters of a mile through a field. I'll show you that field over here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah, you sure?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Three quarters of a mile, we had to dig every 400 feet. Dead man log, 10 foot long, three foot and hard pin. It's an anchor, don't you see? You didn't have to fill a hole up, but you had to have that much, that deep in order to hold it. We never did let one slip. We always had plenty of anchors.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did them old stump pullers work?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: You had a team with a sweep and they pull right around, wind the cable right around your stump puller. When you hooked the one end of the cable over there to your building, she started coming, oh, was I feeling good. Didn't move fast, but that took us about 10 short days. We were 10 short days because we only put in about 5-6 hours a day because we both had a lot of chores late in the fall, in November, cold weather, which I was glad of. I plowed this field, I was pulling right through this field that I'm going to show you, three quarters of a mile, and I was just wishing I could get through it before bad weather because that would have been a mess. Well, we did. We got it right down on some orchard grass, right by the pond, pretty close to where I wanted to set the house. I told my neighbor then, I said, golly, I can handle it now. I said, because I knew there would be a lot of work to it, but that's all I had to do, all the weather, chores, and that was my job. The reason I wanted to close the pond was so I could have handy to water for the salad. Dad had a good pond, but he didn't have a good nut to suit me one winter. There's another thing I want to tell you. One winter, when we had the cattle, my little brother, Joe, was with me. We had to drive our cattle three miles to get to the water.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: That little pond that Dad had froze over, solid. But Rogers had a great big pond, we drove our cattle down there. Once a day is all you could afford to do is cold weather, and they'd drink good once a day and then fed them straw seed. So I said, Joe, next spring we're going to fix that pond. I said, I think I got an idea. You see, you had to dig down a ditch and fill it with clay to make it hold. I said, the water back in the field, but I said, I don't care, I want water. I said, I want this kind of a job no more, which I did. I reed the bank up, see. I forget now, three or four feet.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Just with clay? Just pile of clay?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, no, first clay next to the bank, for the water strip at, you see. About three foot, three or four foot wide bank. That'll hold the water. And then finish filling, you could, if you wanted, had to have to fill your bank.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What time of the year did you get all this?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, this was, we done that late in the fall when the pond was practically dry, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did Dad do it?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: You betcha. Instead of three feet of water in dry weather, I had seven or eight feet of water. Nice, clear water. Dad was smart enough to have a pipe, to pipe it into a tank outside. But then we had another pipe, from that down to the hog lot, with floats in, don't you see? And in Thurman, I didn't have to bother with the water for the sows after they got it, their little pigs got weaned when they got outside. They had the water out there. All I had to do was feed them their grain.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did this clay come from right on the place there?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh yeah, we just dug down, dug off black dirt down the clay and then dug it out. It worked, but by God we did it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you use, did you just do shovels?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh good, we had a team and what they call a slip. That's a two horse thing that, then I think even, no I don't know if we had the, you see they do have a what they call a fresnel four horse scraper. ... We had a two horse, a little handier. You could handle it with two horses. You can do a lot of work with one of them, a couple of guys can. And you can get in narrower places, don't you see? And that's all you had to have, a little there on the bottom, well about as wide as that, three feet, something like that. And it's all one team can do to pull, and when you fill it, pull. Fill that up. I mean I got that all fixed up. Well then one year. The year after I got this house put in, I had these fourteen sows, fourteen petitions off in this house.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I think you told me about how the house made good then. ... Well there's one thing I do want, because I'll try to help you, we'll get the things you wouldn't help me. But on moving that hog house, how did you get it on skid, was that a big job?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, no we had to jack it up. Oh, jack it up, see. Enough so we could work under that. And I had, Dad had timber on the place, and I got a couple of big bold pine trees peeled. Green ones, they were slick. But you see, you peel the bark off, and they would slip along easier. Oh you had to have, they'd bore off anyway, and we'd just peel, I was just peeling before we'd get them under there. God I was young then, I could work like a tiger. I was only, that was you see in 1920, wait a minute now, 23 and 4. See 23 I was what, 23, 35 years old. Man, the work didn't amount to anything for me. I just worked my tailbone off on that ranch, but I tell you I made a go of it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Listen, what I'd like to do is, why don't we go back and kind of start at the beginning and work our way up to here, so I can see it all as a picture. The whole thing in...  Well why don't we start then with the, now I was gonna...

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Wait till I get this pup a drink... I always tell you when a person settles on the ridge.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Are you talking about Central Ridge?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, that's where we live. That's where Dad hopes to, Central Ridge. And see, I was only 8 years old when Dad moved over there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He moved from Park, did he?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yep, with a wagon and a Cayuse team… a Cayuse team… moved, we didn't get more than, we got over on Big Barrage first day. Next day I think we got to, as near as I can remember, either Cavendish or Peck. When we got to Peck, we stayed there. Well, he left us, all the family but me. I went with Dad. I was the oldest, but I was only 8 years old. He took me along anyway. And, he says, God, there was no road up that mountain. You had to go right up that old ridge. The Cayuses couldn't pull a whole wagon, so he just played smart. That's why I say he's a good figurehead. He worked hard, struggled. Now, if he hadn't had a little head on him, he wouldn't have done all that. What he done, he put a pole in this hind wheels. You know, that makes them just like one cart. Hooked his horses on there and all he piled on there was just the cook stove and some dishes. Box of dishes and cook stove. We got to going up this mountain. There was a dog gone steep one place they couldn't pull it, see. Well, Dad unloaded the dishes. And I guess he finally made them pull the stove a little ways, and then he went back and carried the dishes up. I was too little to help him. 8 years old, you know. But he done all the work and I seen him do it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was there even a track for him to follow up the hillside?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, we got up the hill. Well, there's a kind of what they call a saddle after you got about darn two-thirds of the way up the mountain. Kind of a level spot, see. We rested there pretty good.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: No trail or nothing up there?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, nothing… just a mountain side. Just a hill grade. I mean, we call it, I don't know what you would call it, kind of a ridge. They did build a grade later on, see. Farmers got together and cooperated and worked together and shoveled and picked and maybe they had scrapers. I suppose they did because they had quite a grade. They made about a three, four mile grade, see, down, made switchbacks on that grade. That's the old grade.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So you rested two-thirds of the way up and then he got...

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, and when we got home, I was going to tell you that. When we got home, he had a little cab on the homestead that he had... He'd been over here and homesteaded, filed on it, see. You see, he had a little homestead in Park, above where Granddad's place, where Steiner lives now. But he could relinquish them days. You could what they call relinquish. And he played smart. Oh, everybody in Park thought he was a fool, you know, didn't figure he could make it. But he was smart enough that he took this place, he laid it in a Z. He got an 80 land... wait, no, it was east and west here. Here's west. Yeah. He got an 80 land here, east and west. Then another one over here, east and west, that 40 joined... The east 40 joined this west 40, see. So it laid in a Z. Well, this neighbor's place that he bought, as I tell you that I read the beans on, was the 30 or 40 acres that laid in between this... in the corner of this Z.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Filled his place, I'll see. Besides, made a lot of pasture land down in the canyon. That place had 150, 60 acres on it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, why did he pick the east-west? Did that give him all ridge?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, it was the best land with a land laid in between this draw and the canyon.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So it was all on the ridge, more or less on the ridge?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: It's a ridge, that's a ridge. It's called Central Ridge. That's why they had the... So if he'd have took it the other way, he would have gotten canyon, and he didn't know. Oh, he wouldn't have gotten near the land that he got. Oh, you betcha. He played smart, taking it like he did. Okay. And, in a way, he had this little cabin built from these timber that was on there, you see, just a pine log. I think it was about 11 by 12, something like that, and he didn't even have a door. He had just a hole that jumped in and out of just the dirt floor, and he had some sourdough that he had made, was all ready to go, see. Just a minute, Audrey. He'd made. I mean, he had left that. I guess sourdough you can leave for quite a while. It's still good, see. And he had a frying pan. And the only thing else we had to eat was just some fat pork. He didn't fry it very good, but you know how when you get real good, you know, it tastes pretty good. And he's going to be smart, though. He says, now look, he says, I'm going to show you how I can plop them. He didn't play foxy. He'd throw it up like that and melt it and just pound it down the dirt, but we just broke it off. It was good. Tasted good. I can remember that just like it happened yesterday.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: There it was, just a little eight-year-old kid, see… well, another little job he had me doing, and after he got established,… he scratched up 12 acres of ground. He barred a neighbor's horse, so he had three on a little 14-inch plow. Scratched just 12 acres up with. And he butchered a cow long in the winter. I guess he didn't have hay. He had to butcher and kept part of the meat, just part of it, and he traded the rest for some seed to sow this ground the next spring. And the next year, he sold hay off of this piece of ground that he plowed up to help them along. You know how much he made in Harvest Field when he went out? He had to leave all of us there, and no water at home. There wasn't no water on the place. And he left a horse there for us with a couple of syrup kegs on each side of him. We had to go down in the canyon where there was a spring to pack water at.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And us little barefooted boys, that was our summer's job. And so when he'd come home, of course, he'd bought some shoes for us. I guess, I think a dollar, dollar and a half pair of them days. No one of us kids, you know, we'd get out and try to lose this guy. He'd come out there, moonlight night, say, you boys get in the house and take them shoes off. You know, tear them around, you save them for winter. It's just that hard up. Okay, we went and had to obey him. We was little devil's reason. It's all right. He rooted us. And then the next year when he got a little more ground plowed up, so he had enough to sow flax. You know what flax is? And he was just lucky enough to get a good price for that flax. But what I started saying, when he sowed that, he broadcast with his hand this way. Little boy, for about maybe ten years old, man, had to go walk in his tracks so he could see how far he had to go away from it, see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: You know what I mean? So he'd get it lapped just right. And he'd sow this early in the morning, about four o'clock before the breeze would come up, because that flax is light. And the breeze will blow it. There I was just talking on barefoot in the cold, Jesus barefoot, in the wooly morning.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You, he was following, you would be in the next morning?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, I'd go ahead of him. Oh, yeah. This is the track. Away from me. You know, that way, he'd laugh. Jesus, he got a good job seeding that way. Later years then, here's another improvement they made over that. Right here, he got the idea. Somebody, I guess, had done it, and he'd seen it. On these two hind wheels that I was telling you about, how it fixed, you know. Locked them. He put a tub, a wash tub, put grain in that, and he had me driving the team. No, had one of us boys driving the team, the other one on a pony out here, riding the wheel tracks with a rope to the horses. So they couldn't know no beat just so far. And Dad, of course, when he was standing, he'd stand there and sew with both hands, broadcast both ways, he could sew 40 feet wide. He could sew 40 acres a day that way.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He'd stand in the back of the wagon?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: He'd stand in the back of the wagon, grab his wheat out of this grain, and go this way. Forty acres a day. Well then, we had to harrow that to get it covered so it grew. Later years, then he finally got him a broadcast signal. They got little shovels, and there's only about eight or ten foot of them, but Dad didn't sew near fat. But you could sew, oh, well, you had to go like the devil. You'd go 20 acres a day with that four horse. Three or four. Three horses, I think, are all they pulled out that way. Listen, you asked me, I know how much you made in harvest that first year, and you didn't tell me what happened in that first year of harvesting when he went out. Oh, I forgot that. $35. That's what he got.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long did he go?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, God, not very long. Well, that was $35. Hell of a wage. Well, of course, he was a stacker, but I don't know if he stacked that year, though. See, later years, when the farmers started to get in bigger fields, and they found out Dad was a good stacker, they harrowed him right and left. I had to go helping to pitch. When I was 15 years old, I took a man's place, boy. I was out there pitching them big bundles on the stacks, but I'm not sure of the stacks he got there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he work around Genesee or someplace? Do you know where he went to work that year?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, Genesee country. Yeah, he worked in the Genesee country. They were more advanced than farmers, see. Excuse me, I've got to go to the bathroom. Go ahead.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How was it that your folks wound up leaving Norway and coming to park? You mean my folks coming from Norway?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah. Oh, yeah… you see, Dad was only five years old when the grandparents come over the ocean, see. And they settled in—you want me to tell where they settled? ... They settled in Minnesota. And they stayed there a while. And Dad didn't get married until he was 25, see. He got to working out after he got—I guess to be quite a little man, a young man, you know, and saving his money. Them days, people would save their money better than they do nowadays. Well, they had to. And Granddad had to haul oak poles. I think he said nine miles they had to go get this with oxen. He didn't have much transportation with oxen, see. And they stayed there and they had bad luck. But Dad was smart. He worked out for wages. He wasn't farming. Didn't get big wages, but he kept saving what he could, see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: They had bad luck with the oxen and the hogs?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, no. No, no. No, they had bad luck with the crops. That's what I want to tell you later. Maybe I shouldn't tell you about this hard luck he had getting his wood. He said it took them—they'd go start 9 o'clock in the morning and go back to him and his brother. He was a husky man, old Granddad. He lived to be 97, sickest he ever saw of us. He stayed with us one winter over there in Park, where he was on the corn place. And coming up behind me, you know, like that, walking. Hammer, just getting talked to, playing. You would haul the logs down here. He says, I will cut them up. I carried the wood in them days we burned wood, see. And cook stove and all. Well, I said, Granddad, I said, I did have a tree climber, they call it. You've seen them tree climbers, all wood saws, ain't you? That I had traded a gang plow that I brought from the ridge. Oversea, it fell in there in Park, had it. And traded even up. So I had this gas wood saw and there was a great big tree up in the mountainside there. Well, Granddad, if I cut this big log, I can't snake it down, but I said I saw the blocks up and I'd bring them down here and you split them up.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, yes, that'd be all right, he said. But he did saw the little logs. He's smart enough to hold up on skids, see. And he'd stand straight. And I could file a saw because I'd learned that when I was cutting cordwood the first year we was married in Orofino. 1914. That's how I made my living that winter was cutting cordwood. Dollar in a quarter of a cord. So your grandfather, he was pretty old and... Well, he was about as old as Stein. There is now about 85 or 65 years old. Already. But hell, he was a husky. God, he was out there working like that, see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Right when he was out there?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah. So he said, I fell this tree and knocked down five others. It was luck to have it. The little ones got in the way, see. But it made it nice. It laid in a hill like that in the upper part of the tree. The stump part laid up the hill and I just could move my saw down the hill, see. And I hauled the blocks down. Oh, hell, he was four or five foot in diameter. Great bed blocks. But it made good ... It was yellow pine.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Okay, but you were talking about him and his logging when he was a young man himself.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, he didn't know. Well, you want me to finish? Yeah, I am getting too far ahead. Now we jumped from Minnesota Park again. Okay, we'll finish Minnesota now. The way it was, he got his wood that way. Him and his brother, Throne, he called him. They would go out there and he said they could saw. No, they didn't saw them days. They just chopped that oak. It was hard to saw. And them saws they had them days wasn't a good saw. It was just them hands off. No drag team. And I guess they didn't even. So they made headway by chopping. He was a very good action man. Oh God, they just chopped four cards. Of course, that would be four foot length. They said they could make four cards in a day from go there and come back. Took them six hours, see, to do all that and make that nine mile trip. That's a ... They had to go like the devil to do all that work and make all that trip nine miles. I don't know how they done it, but that's what he claimed he done.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: They was farming there for four or five years. Two years I think it was… they had hailstorms… either two years hailstorm or three years hailstorm and vice versa. Grasshoppers. Five years hard luck. And Dad, he had enough money saved up that I guess he could move all of them, grandparents and all, over the park. See, they found out there's homesteads in the park. And this granddad of mine, of course, he was a husky and then he'd go out in Harvest Field too. And he was a good stacker. That's why he come to get to make a go of it. Every summer he'd come out here to Genesee country, stack grain for the people. And in the winter, he would sit there and split shakes. That's what Ed was telling about, how he carried them shake blocks, you remember? They didn't have horses. They made snowshoes to walk on top of the snow. Put them shakes, see. He'd do that in park. Yeah, that was in park. Now, you would think that a man wouldn't go across to an old canyon. There wasn't no grave there then, see. But he just loved that country. What he was after was the timber. He got all that cold stuff in the east that no timber close, you see. He wanted to get with his plenty of timber close. And beside the water. He got a, he was smart enough to find a good spring on that place. That's still there.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Water and wood. He had her mate.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you know where it was in Minnesota, more or less, where they were at?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, it was close to Minneapolis. Let's see, what do they call that? Let's see now. It was, yeah, Minneapolis, I believe, was their closest place. Pretty close. And there was, see, let me look at my birth certificate. This, looky there. I got those carpentry bikes calling. I took up welding first. And I only lasted on it, I mean it got the best of me. Here it is. Yeah, here it shows. Swift Falls, Minnesota. That's what I try to think of. That's where it was. See.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did your grandfather ever talk to you about why it was that he left Norway and come to Minnesota?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: God damn it, he started that back there. Yet they had what they called, that's how Dad come to get the name, you know, his name. See, Dad's name was Swenson too, like Addison. They're full of brothers. But Dad, he gets a little bit better than the rest of them. A little more brainy, I guess you'd call it. He went and, he was all time reading. He hadn't got much education, but by God, he read. And he took up, there on the ridge, he got the idea that the farmers should organize and start a farmers mutual fire insurance company by their own. Which Dad started there in Nez Perce County. See what I mean? That's what he started. And he'd go canvassing around, he left us boys to do the farming. He'd give us orders what to do. But he kept us together. Five of us boys. After Mother died, she died in 1901. Seventy-five years ago.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So, this was a cooperative for all the farmers?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, Dad organized it that way. And he said it like this. He only charged a dollar and a half of policy, but they would be assessed according to whatever loss there was. Like if there was a hundred farmers, we'll illustrate. A hundred farmers belonged. Alright, if one poor fella lost, say, five thousand dollars by fire, these other farmers would club together and pay that loss. And that was a lot cheaper way of getting along than it was to go into these big companies. That company now, of course, is in the big hands now. Somebody got wise and made a little more money on it and kept fooling the four farmers. She's big cooperative now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, what did that have to do with him changing his name?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, that's what I come to tell you. Dad, after he got Brother Edward and Brother Gilbert, both moved over there, and Granddad. That's three Swensons, and his and his four. And his mail would get mixed up pretty bad. Don't you see the mail care? He'd get his mail, Dad's mail, and so that Dad wanted this old, this was the old name, I mean the name of the old place. It had an R on it, Ring Sejour, Rings Aachen in Norwegian we call it. That's eight weeks. And so he, of course, he had to pay for it. He went to Lewiston, found a seat, and he got, he cost him $40, but us boys could change before our name, before we had real estate. And the first year we went to school in Spokane, like I told you, getting that college there, I didn't finish that. There we finished, I was 22, Sandra was 20. We finished the seventh and eighth grade in eight months. That's the longest term we ever had. We had a private teacher, and I never knew Grammer when my bones felt, she illustrated, and I can understand. Oh, I wouldn't know that. Oh, they probably read papers or news gets around, see. Hard to tell how they found that out. But anyway, that's about how old he was.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: He was 20, I mean, they had lived in Minnesota about, what did I say? Twenty-three years. Yeah. So they struggled there for quite a little while, you see. But you say, you say. Twenty-three years, that was the worst, see. That's when they had that tough time. That's what convinced them to get out of there, I guess.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You say that people were starving in Norway.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I mean, people were really... Well, yeah, I don't know. They just wanted to get out. They had no future. Just, you know what Norway is, little old stipple land along the, you got to, that's where Granddad got to have it eaten. Excuse me. He could eat the fattest fish and pork. He could eat boiled fat pork. He got that happy, see. But he just naturally helped Uncle Ed. His youngest son said that he must have had a good bile or whatever you call it, the digestion of the fat stuff.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Okay, well, when your father got to park, when he got to park, did they take a homestead there?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: He took a little homestead above where Grandpa was, he is, right above him, in the lower edge of that mountain.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember about that?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, I don't remember that time much. It was all, everything was after we moved to the ridge, see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, now why was it that he decided to go to the ridge and leave park? Now what was the difference?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, Jesus, quite the big prairie land instead of that old timber brush land. Who wouldn't? Would you do it? Would you do it?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Sure, if it was all, it wasn't no timber on the top of Central Ridge, it was...

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, he had enough timber in that little draw there. He had it for firewood. That's all he wanted. But the top of the ridge was... The rest of the land was all 160 acres of farmland. You mean it was prairie before he... Prairie land is what it was. It was the next first Indian reservation. Got opened up. There's a while that wasn't opened up, see, for settlement. And the government allowed them to get a homestead free and open up the charge. All they had to do was to improve it. Get on there and plow it up and make something out of it. By golly, my old little old daddy did, besides making us little devils help him. And that was all right. You made men out of us. By golly. And then, you see, they got there and... Oh, Dad, I didn't tell you about that. I don't know whether you want to put that all in or not. But, see, on the ridge then, when we get going, he started raising horses.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: That's why, where he made these ones. Them days, everything was farmed with horses. Boy, he had awful good luck with horses. He had, oh, he'd have four, maybe six colts sometimes. And he'd sell them to farmers that didn't raise them. And they brought all the way from 250 to 300 dollars a horse, them days. Hadn't been for that horse raising, he never would have got in that place, because grain wasn't much. He just fed that doggone stuff to the horses and made money on the horses. That's what he used his ... But going into horses. machinery, of course, then when I got to farming, that was clear out. Everybody started with machinery. But I had, I farmed with horses.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How come these other folks in Park thought he was crazy to go to a new country?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, dammit, they didn't, just couldn't see the future over there. Like Dad did, see. No, they just, my uncle, I had two uncles on my mother's side. Steiner was one of the names, he joined this, yeah, he joined this granddad place there, 140 of his land joined on the north, his north 40. He took his land north and south. This uncle, Uncle Helle, he had a nice place. That was really the best place in Park, almost. Laid a lot of it level, but it was a little bit on the wet side, swampy. It was nice from the level. And you see whoever come in there first, their choice, you know what I'm saying, on them homesteads, just like they did on the ridge. I heard Ed Swenson told me that there was one guy they called the Land Grabber. There was one guy there that took a lot of good land in the bottom. Well, I don't know who that would have been at the time, let's see. Oh, it doesn't matter. Well, I'll tell you, they sold out, but they couldn't homestead more than one quarter, you know. That's all they could do. Well, I guess from what you're telling me, Park just didn't have the potential that other places had. Oh, no, that's just a small place compared to, well, you know, the central ridge. When you get up towards Nez Perce, there's all that Craigmont country. That spreads out wider. And then there's another ridge to the east of where we lived called Russell Ridge, another one to the west called Melrose Ridge, and then another little ridge down beyond that north of it called Angel Ridge.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And then, well, here I want to tell you how Dad started. Getting that flag. There was no railroad in fact I'd own for several years. But his flags, by delivering it to Kendrick, he got two and a quarter or two and a half a bushel. And it wasn't very, I guess, but God, he couldn't haul much. He only had two little coyotes just to haul with him. Quite a wagon was put in there alone because they had to go up that, they went down the path, up the sunny side, Clearwater side, on top of American, or Big Potlatch, down to Kendrick in that Kendrick grade to get to the Kendrick warehouse. It took him putting here a week to make one trip. Now can't you imagine that Dad was struggling? That's what told the story. By God, he had to have a lot of guts to do all that. And not only guts, but strength. I said, the man doing all that, I said, he was alone then, he had to do all the man work. The week it wasn't big enough at that time. I said, my God, he was struggling. Boy, I tell you he was struggling.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Then, to do his harvesting, all he had was a six foot binder with three horses on it. That pulled it to a certain extent. Then he had one old mare, she said, God damn, every time you hit her, you know, she'd speed up a little bit and then she'd... That old bun... I could hear that thing. Oh, Dad come in and be hot, you know. Luck could have it though, they'd learn to keep cows. You know what he done when he got in when it was hot? Have you got this one? Yeah, yeah. Come in to get something to drink that was quenching. Got over to the pan of sour milk, clavered milk, drink. You just could figure make a meal on that sour milk. Then when us boys got big enough to do the shocking, we had to get out and shock up the bunters. When Dad and Mother died, let's see, that was when I was 13, 14 years old. You betcha, we shocked them, we was working like mad. See, I was plowing when I was 11 years old.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: With one of them footman's, I plowed that whole ranch for three or four years until I was about 16 before he got a gang plow. I couldn't drive four horses, you see, before that. But I'd practice driving these four horses because he and me go down and water his horses. He'd go out and harness them, see, and feed them early in the morning before breakfast. Then come in and get his breakfast while I go out there and hitch them up for him. Well, I thought here's a good chance to drive four horses. If it wasn't hooked onto anything, I'd hitch them up, get them watered, hitch them up. I'd practice pulling the lines this horse and that horse. Pretty soon I got confidence in myself. I told Dad, I says, you can get a gang plow now. I said, I can drive four horses. He says, you think you can. I said, you betcha.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I said, I'll handle them on a gang plow, anyway. Sure enough, you did. Then I got to plowing around this big field, half my log, you know, which was a nice field. And got into a straw bottom.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: A what?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Straw bottom. Now that's the old plow plug up. I didn't have a fortune in the field. I learned something there. I didn't. Boy, I didn't go close to a straw bottom anymore. And another thing, I could ride that thing, see. I didn't have to handle stuff. I could stand and ride if I wanted to. See what I mean… that's easy work… the only work I had was to harness a horse, if you can harness a horse. Well, this said, this straw, straw bottom.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How deep would the straw be?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh, it depends on it. You see, if the cattle were either down, or just being piled up, they'd maybe tromp down towards three feet of it. And that's what I thought I'd go through. I mean, go over. I figured I'd go over. It didn't go over. It didn't grab it. It plugged it up when it done. So then I stayed shy. Yeah, I went around it. You were doing all this work with the walking plow. That's because you were... Well, that was from 11 until I was 16, 15 or 16.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now, why did you do that? That's because your dad was out selling...

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, he was probably out canvassing. Yeah, he was out canvassing. Or maybe fencing. That place. He had to fence that place all by himself. Make his wood as timber, and post. That's what I told Tyler. He thinks he's doing something fencing. I said, Mr. Steiner, you got a little old dinky 80 acres. I said, you've got to have had it all fenced here for years. Poor daddy had to fence all that, and I was the instigator to coax him to put hog wire on. He never raised a hog in his life. Hadn't been that he had that hog wire on. I probably wouldn't have raised a hog, but because he had it, I got the idea and went in and raised and made money on it… the first years… no, I told you the first year I didn't make it. Second year, second year, 23. That's the time I want to tell you… 1923… yeah, that's the first year. I had good luck. 14 showers brought me 109 pigs. Now, you told me. Yeah, well, I saved them.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: I mean, I saved them. I saved 105, but I had to borrow $500 to feed them over to my grain trash. I guess, did I tell you that a door once? ... Well, then you got that. Well, that was it. And then, the next year, I didn't have good luck. But, as I said, that last year, that's when I borrowed that. You see, on summer follow, I had half corn, half peas. And I would hog the peas first, because they'd come on first. Little Alaskans. And as soon as they were done, by that time, the corn would be plenty ripe and the pigs would go right into it. And by then, the place, the fence hog dug, I'd just turn the hog loose. The only thing, they had to come over to the pond to get their water, but that's all they had to do. Go over back and fill up and come and, maybe in the middle of the day, when it was hot, they'd come and drink up. And then they'd go along in the evening, go out and fill up again.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, hell, it worked slick. And so that year, as I said, though, I didn't have quite as many. I only had, instead of 105, I saved, I think it was about 85 pigs. Because I let the fruit sows run with the fattening hogs, and they got too fat, so they didn't have good luck with their pigs. But I did save that many, and the price come up. See, the first year that I barred the 500, I only got six, six and a half cents a pound.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But this next year, the price come up?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: The next year, the price come up. First half, I sold, I got eight and a half. And the other half, you see, you couldn't sell them all at the same time, because some of them didn't mature quite as good. And the other half, I got ten and a half. Well, that brought me 44, I mean, put me out of debt. I was in debt $4,400. Besides, I had a little money left to live on, and I told that little banker, and all, said, oh, you're just getting good started. They figured I was doing fine. I'd paid the bank up, you see. And I was able to pay that up, and I said, I want to get out. I've been there seven years struggling like mad. I was just about peddled out. I didn't weigh over 130, 140 pounds. I'll tell you why. The mister was sick that spring. I had the summer fall, about last summer fall I was telling you about, that I barred, I wouldn't have got anything off of that ground. I didn't get a planter. It plowed early.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: It dried up in May. And this west, well, his name is Wesley Thomas, John, I call him, that theory. He was living on his dad's place, or his uncle's place, Wesley Thomas, was his uncle's name. And he had this steel roller packer. And I got the idea then that God and this ground was so bad, plowed a great big chunk, and I had a double disc, seven horses on it. That's what I had to farm with so I could plow the ground when it was dry, see. And that would chop the clods up, but it didn't pack it the way I wanted it, because I wanted to put peas in, and you've got to have ground in good shape for peas, and corn. And it was so dry, along about the 12th of May. And I got over to Thomas, I said, how about hiring your roll? Go ahead and take it, he says, I'm through with it. See, he had got his crop all in.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: So I went and used it, and I just rolled it and packed it, and then I'd disc it and harrow it and pack it again. And I just had that doggone ground just packed and worked up pretty good, near the best I could. Then I planted my peas and my corn. It took till the 42 life or any of that come up, and I thought, well, gee whiz, if I get something, I'll be lucky. No rain! But there was moisture in the bottom. That land was rich. And in the winter, it would absorb this subsoil below, would hold it, if there's enough moisture in the winter to go down. You see, I hadn't plowed, no, by God, that's something I hadn't plowed before. I generally did plow my ground in the fall. But I hadn't come around to it. But you let go through spring. I was too busy, for some reason, or froze up or something. And there that spring, I had two mares going to fold, and the wife was sick of that. She brought birth to a dead baby boy, 10 pounds. Putting her diet with him.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: The name of.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So it didn't work out as being any better?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, that didn't pan out at all. I had to quit, and I went harvesting. I tell you, I worked for Jeff Stanford, the next one, in harvest. I got two and a half a day there, and bored. For 12 hours work, and he had a header. And I drove header box. So then, I stayed there all summer. Well, Dad, he was pretty good. That learned him a good lesson. Now, he got smart to help Steiner. Steiner stayed home. So he told him, and he told me, he wanted this cash that I had made, because I didn't have enough to go to Canada on. And Dad would hard run. And he said, now he says, I'll sell you boys a cow apiece, and you get the offspring, and you'll just be increasing that one… well, we agreed… we stayed there and worked. Kept getting cattle ahead, see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You mean you gave up the idea of going?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, I gave up because I couldn't make money enough to go up there to Canada. And Dad fixed it that way. He kind of wanted to settle it down. He guess he figured that he didn't like the lettuce. Let me go clear up there and try to struggle in that cold country, I suppose. That's what he figured. So we stayed with that… that was 1906… and you, uh... And then, wait. 1906. Let's see, what was it? 1907. Dad took a notion. He was studying. He'd learned about it. In Moscow, and he could get to go to school, finish up his high school at the university, which he did. Now, he passed his high school at Moscow University. He's a good-looking boy there. Now, here's Dad. See, 1908 was. First, I'll have to tell you, about 19... Yeah, I don't... Let's see, 1907. Yeah, it was 1907, I guess, that Dad was building the house. I'll show you after a while. He got the carpenters. He had this fellow that he bought oats from up on the ridge.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: They were Fredericksen. They were good carpenters. And Dad, then they didn't have to pay, oh, $2,000 a day. It was a big wage. And he was hard running. He only had a small farm, 40 acres up there on the ridge. So he was glad to get some work, you know. But he was a good carpenter, and Dad knew it. And Dad got him to build his house and also the barn. In 1908, they had got the barn built, and that's when I wanted to tell you. Here he is. He took off to go to this school. Wait, now, I'll find him pretty soon. Here he is. That's my Dad.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Which school is that?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, that's Weltner School. That's chiropractor. He got the idea. He wanted to take that up. And he did. He passed on it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Fair back to Missouri. And he had rented a place to Stein. Stein and Evani was 1908. I was, uh, wait a minute, I was 21 then… yeah… 12 years on the 8th. Yeah, I was 20. Stein was 18. And, uh, but I just, I didn't want to rent it, people. I didn't know why Dad wanted to rent it to him, but he did. And, uh, he went back to Missouri. He went back to Missouri, left us boys there. And, uh, I wanted to keep working out whenever I had time. I helped Stein on the farm while he had a boy there named Lee Galloway to help him plow. Them days, I think, then the, let's see, 1918. Well, we had, uh, 1908. We had gang plow. I don't know, maybe, oh, I know. He was running a gang plow and a walking plow. That's what he was doing. That's what he was doing, because I knew we had gang plow and there were lots of horses.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was your father's interest in chiropractors?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, because he thought that he could make, being a, as boys, big enough to do the farming, and he'd go out and do little stuff, which he did. He went over to Kendrick one year and practiced. And then, when I started, when he rented out to me, after I was married, you know, 1917, then he pulled it, well, he went to Kirkland, Washington, bought a house and lot there. And the grandparents stayed with us that summer, till fall.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And, because Uncle Ed, let's see, was he sold out?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah. See, Uncle Ed had already sold out. So, the grandparents had to, that was the trick that Ed played on Dad. He first got Dad the promise to take care of the old parents for $1200, and yet Dad had helped him get that place over there. He furnished, I mean, he bought this property over here to park for $2200, Dad did, to give him a down payment on that place. And then, Ed was lucky. That last year that he farmed, he got $2000 worth of beans off the place, and he got $8000 from the place, and it only cost him $5000 to begin with. He got reckless with that money and he went down to southern Idaho, where my aunt, his sister, lived, and Albert Stanford, and started in with some cattle, but they couldn't make it. It was a dry country, so he didn't stay there long. He just let it go, and then he got the bright idea to go to camp.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now, is that the one that killed his wife?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: That's the one, yeah. Yeah, he killed his wife. He finally shot her with a rifle, and then he took his own life in the night.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you hear? Did you hear about what happened?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, the people, the relatives told me, Uncle Jim, they found out, you know, news scatters, you know. Yeah, that goes like wildfire, something like that, you know. Yes, he was jealous of her. She had to go out with the neighbor lady in a buggy. And they were all heaps of ... I knew something wrong with the old bastard when I was there, but I was kind of a bully sort of a guy, French-Canadian, you know. They were pretty hot-headed. And so I just, I was glad to get out of there. Geez, I got over there to Swanson's. They were nice people.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was he mean when you worked with him?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: No, he didn't order me around any. He didn't do that. And he seemed that that was when they first married. He was pretty sweet to each other then, don't you see? But this was, I don't know, a year or two years after when he shot her, that they got on the out with each other for some reason. He got jealous of her going with the neighbors, women, talking. I don't know, maybe someone was, pretty mouth-piercing. And he'd overheard something that made him mad, don't you see?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But the other thing I was going to ask you is, now did your father ever, did he do much practicing of chiropractic?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, he did. You see, he went, he done a little in Idaho, in Kendrick, but when he got out to Kirkland Martin, he had to take different licenses out there. But he practiced out there, too. You betcha. He had a lot of time. He was, well, like I said, I farmed his place seven years.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And he was practicing all that time?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, he was practicing what he could. And Granddad, he had him there then, and before Grandma died, that was before 1922, that he, Granddad was cutting wood for him. They had wood around there, you see. And I guess he had a fireplace or something that he was feeding the neighbors. He might have been cutting wood, but I don't remember that. So he believed in chiropractors. Oh yeah, I tell you, he's helped out. Now I tell you, one time he did help me out. I was, let's see, that was after he'd done that, but that was before I got married. I was helping him haul alfalfa hay in. This barn, he had had hay shoots to shove the hay down, you know, down to the feed walkway, feed way. And I was up in the mile, Dad was down there unloading with slings. We had slings, two or three slings to a load of hay. And I was up there placing the hay around and telling him when to strip it. Well, I stepped back like that, didn't see, you know, in a hurry. There was a little loose hay on this shooting up there with my head, I mean, ass down.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Lit right on my head. Come on. Put me down there, Jesus. Land all my weight right on my tailbone and the bone walked. Dad hollered at me, said, what's the matter? He said, you up in the mile? What's going on? I said, oh Dad, I fell down the hay shoot and I said, I can't get up. By God, he come in there and he treated me for about a half an hour on my back and down my tailbone. By God, he took me out of it. And I learned from then on that that was quite a bit to it, that nerve. He treated the nerves, see.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did he do? Did he massage you down there?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Massage me good. And so it hadn't been for him and I never did get over it right away, but it started me. It took me out of that shock, see. Him knowing something about nerve treatments. It took me out of that shock and I went right back toward him. Only half an hour that he had to treat me until I was right back up there placing the hay. Finished holding his hay. Another thing, I didn't tell anyone, well maybe we better leave that until next time. When he went to eat to get to school, that's when we leave off. Then I painted the barns because he had the carpenters leave those castles up there. We'll start on that. I had the targets and girls and her name was Emma Gullingford. And she was good, just followed by the Norwegians. She could talk Norwegian good, but I couldn't. I could understand it, see. Because I always talked to Emma in Norwegian, so I could talk it plenty good so we could understand one another. She wanted to be dead, but she liked the coffee. She thought I'd have it. I just didn't cooperate, but she needed some.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: See, I had a lot of chances when I was young, you know. But anyway, we were dancing away because this was good music. We danced from one room into the other. That's how we danced. Small room, see, probably as big as this. And you'd just dance from one room all around in this and then you'd move into the other. The whole crowd did the same thing. It was just a lot of fun. And these, Fritz Olson and Willie Osborn, they were playing violin. And I think, I forget now whether it was a ... or a harp of some kind that Fritz was playing for second music. Oh, you just couldn't sass it. You had a waltz, they'd just pull you around, you know. When them old timers played them waltz, I tell you, that really moved your legs if you had any waltz in you. And we'd learned, Steiner and I had learned dancing on the ridge when we was kids. See, my aunt used to cook for Dad after Mother's Day.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: We were just kids, but all the neighbor women over there would learn, would love to dance with us kids just because they felt sorry for us. We were, you might say orphans, no mother, so they'd never turn us down. We'd go and ask them and they'd just say, well, one lady especially, Mrs. Malcolm, her husband didn't even dance on the floor for some reason. And she was a good dancer. I always got her to dance. And it was the McBride.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This was, were these dances in homes on Central Ridge too? On Central Ridge, were they having dances in people's homes too?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, that's where it was. ... Just like around Deary. I said, that's where we learned. Yeah. Yeah, we'd go from one neighborhood to the other and once in a while we'd go clear up what they call, Woolworth. That was a little country town, you know, between Nez Perce and Craigmont. It was kind of a little bit north. And this test support, this Dutch kid, you know, he said, come on up, Helmer. He said, sometime we'll go out there, they're going to have a mass parade. He didn't have mass parade dancers. So he can tell who they were. Oh, God, we had a hell of a good time that night, see. And there's all kinds of young people there. God, and he had a sister, you know, Laura. I'd dance with her and all the rest of them. And they all mixed. God, there was no high-hat going on. Everybody got busy and enjoyed themselves.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: See what I mean? Just like we did at Deary. We did that too. I used to, when we lived in Park, we used to go over to Cedar Creek once in a while. And the Cedar Creek folks would come to Park, dance in our schoolhouse there. That's what we did there. And over on Cedar Creek, there was Smith's. Did you ever hear the Smith's over on Cedar Creek?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I think I heard that name.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: It used to be Ben Smith and George Smith were the two boys. And Eva Smith, she's the one that became the owner of the home place. They lived just across from the Longfellow place, if you remember where the Longfellow place was.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So she used to dance with them?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, we danced in Smith's house. They had a big house. And she was a good dancer. She was a big woman, but by God, she was easy on her feet. Oh God, I could dance waltzes with her just like nothing. Just finding dandy. She finally moved down to either Clarkson or Lewiston and became a nurse, I guess.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This masquerade dance, everybody got dressed up until they were born?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Well, yeah, that was the masquerade over there. No, I'm thinking of that one. But the masquerade, yeah, that was. Oh, you bet. That was lots of fun. We just tore around together, you know. And of course, after lunchtime, then they'd fill the masquerade off. You wouldn't know who the hell you had for a partner, see? I think sometimes you'd be buying baskets too, you know. Basket socials and so on.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You bid on it?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, you bid on it. You wouldn't know who your partner was until you got the mask off. Sometimes you'd get what you wanted, sometimes you wouldn't. Then you ate your lunch with the person that fixed it. Oh yeah, if you bought a basket from somebody, you had to eat your lunch with that person, regardless. There's no lady, that didn't matter. You'd eat dinner with her anyway. But there wasn't many old ladies out there, dancers. Most of the young ones, they're mad ladies, but that was all right.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long did these dances go? Did they go late into the night?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Oh yeah, sometimes by God we wouldn't get home until daylight. You'd take the Fourth of July especially, we'd go to Peck, Idaho. And then we didn't come home until daylight, you know. But we were trying to sleep in the daytime, you'd hear that. Oh, I let it go, you couldn't go to sleep.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You were trying to sleep after the dance?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, after the dance, at home in daylight. You just couldn't talk good. And old Dad, you know, uh oh, when we was down in the ridge, just learning. Next morning, you know, after we'd been dancing, we'd be in the bed maybe a couple of hours, just nice sound of sleep. Dad would come up and holler, come on boys, get your chores done. The way we snuck out, see Auntie told us, Dad didn't want us to go to the dance. She said, we'll put a ladder up here. She was two years old now, I see. Put a ladder up upstairs where we walked up.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That was some of the first dancing you done?

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: Yeah, that was when we was first learning. Oh, I guess we were little devils, but thank God, I mean, I went through it all. And I'm glad I didn't get a kick out of it, I'm thinking about it. What a hell of a good time I have had in my younger days. These lunches, by the way, they had real good feeds. Oh, they had cakes and donuts, and sometimes they'd have some cooked beans or something like that, you know. What do you call them, baked beans? Oh, you bet. They were really fat. Country people, you know, they could bring on them old farm ladies. They could cook good, I tell you. They knew what a farm boy eat. They could have bought a plant too. The whole family would go. Oh, no, no. No, well, Mal Malcolm, his children were too small, see, so it'd just be him and his wife. And them boys were over there. That man started out there. There was a nice, nice company. He come to that ridge, he didn't homestead. He had to buy the land. He bought a quarter, no, 80 acres. An old man McKay, and then he bought Kay McKay's 80. There was two boys and the old man, three 80s. Then when he got able, he bought the other man's 80.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: That was Dennis McKay. Well, Rod Pfeiffer had bought one of them 80s, see. Well, later on then, he got... Oh, Malcolm was a prosperous guy. He raised his own horses. He had a stallion of his own. And he was pretty prosperous. He was a good farmer. And his wife, a hard worker, and they got up early. They had long ways to haul the market, see. They were five years, five miles up the ridge, and then five miles to Peck from there. They had a ten-mile haul when they all grew. But anyway, old Malcolm, he had this money ready for this Pfeiffer place, and he bought that. That made it 248. And he had my brothers, Julius and Simon, helping him plow. He had two six-horse teams, gang plows, black perchings. And he hired them boys. Them days, dollar a day, it was big money. Dollar a day in both. They plowed and took care of the horses the best they could. And they became good friends with Malcolm's, and he'd hire them every spring, see.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: To help plow, because he could depend on Simon, especially. The only trouble with Simon was the sleepy head. He was hard to wake up in the morning. But Julius wasn't. Julius had come right up. So that's the way it went, and later years after we moved away, they kept... Well, his boys grew up too. He had two boys and a daughter. And she married a farmer over on Angel Ridge that had a farm. So she was gone, but the two boys stayed, and the old folks, they just kept building up. The boys helped, helped, helped. And they got into this modern machinery, and they could start grabbing more land, you see. You know, if you got one section of land, or half a section, the farm wouldn't... You buy another section, half a section, this and that makes two sections. You could pay it lots quicker, and he was smart enough to figure that out.

segments.speaker: Helmer Ringsage
segments.words: And that's the way he kept going. Today them boys are farming, the last I heard, they were farming 1,600 acres. And of course, they got a lot of grandchildren. They're all grown up, and now it's the grandchildren taking over. See, the oldest boys, well, he's around, now see, the youngest boys are around 65. He's as young as I am, quite a bit, about 20-some years. But the oldest boy, he's little older, he's about, I guess about 70. It looks to me like that clock. Yeah, it's one o 'clock. It looks like it's stopping. Oh, quarter after one, yeah it is, I haven't warmed it. I've got to wind it.
